opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer starts with a frustration I had with myself. When I look back at how I actually do research, a huge fraction of what makes an experiment work isn't in any paper I've written. It's things like: which toy model do I reach for first, how small can I make the dataset before the phenomenon disappears, when do I trust a weird loss curve versus when do I suspect a bug, what plots do I make before I even think about the main result. That kind of knowledge lives in my head and in my habits, and it's very hard to transmit. Papers are the polished end product; the know-how is the messy process that got me there.

So one motivation is just preservation and transmission. If I mentor a student, I can sit with them for months and they slowly absorb this taste. But that doesn't scale, and a lot gets lost. If I can write down, as explicitly as possible, the heuristics I use, and put them into something like a language model that can act on them, then in a sense I'm making my research style executable. Someone else, or the model itself, can run with it.

The second motivation is more selfish, but I think also more interesting scientifically. The act of externalizing forces me to understand my own process. Many times I believed I had a principle, and when I tried to articulate it for the model, I realized it was actually three different rules that conflict in certain cases, or that it only made sense because of some context I'd never stated. So it's a bit like the physics habit of trying to write down the equations: you discover what you don't actually understand.

And third, I'm genuinely curious about what AI-assisted science can look like. There's a lot of talk about AI scientists that just do everything end to end. I'm somewhat skeptical of that framing, at least right now. I think a more realistic and more useful path is to take a human researcher's know-how, make it explicit, and let the model amplify it: run many more small experiments than I could, explore variations, and report back in a way that matches how I think. Then I stay in the loop on the parts where taste really matters, like deciding what question is worth asking.

So it's partly about scaling myself, partly about understanding myself, and partly an experiment in what the right division of labor between humans and models in research should be.

fable-5.1.text:
A lot of it is honestly selfish at the start. When I was doing KAN, I noticed that most of what made the project work never showed up in the paper. The paper has the architecture and the results. But the real decisions were things like: this training run looks weird, do I trust it or kill it? This ablation is going to take three days, is it worth it? Which of the twenty ideas on my whiteboard do I try first? That kind of judgment lives in my head, and it's fragile. I forget my own reasoning six months later.

So the first motivation is just to not lose it. If I can write it down in a form that a model can actually use, not just a diary, but something that changes how the model behaves when it faces a similar situation, then I've compressed years of trial and error into something that persists.

The second motivation is that I think experimental taste is the actual bottleneck in science right now, not compute and not ideas. Everyone has ideas. What's rare is knowing which experiment will be informative, and knowing when a result is telling you something versus when it's noise. Senior researchers have that, and they transmit it very slowly, through advising one student at a time over five years. That's an incredibly lossy channel. If a language model can absorb even part of it, you can give that taste to a first-year PhD student on day one.

And the third thing, which I'll admit is more speculative, is that I want to see what happens when you externalize it. Taste feels like intuition, like something you can't articulate. But every time I've forced myself to explain to a student why I'd run experiment A before B, there was a reason. It just hadn't been verbalized. So part of this is an experiment on myself: how much of what I call intuition is actually structured knowledge that I never bothered to write down? My guess is more than I think. And if the model can reproduce my decisions on cases it hasn't seen, that tells me something about what research skill really is.

astra-6.text:
A lot of experimental know-how is tacit. When I’m doing research, I make decisions about what to try next, which results look suspicious, or when to abandon an idea. But a paper usually only presents the final, clean story. The process that got us there is much harder to communicate.

I want to externalize that knowledge so it becomes something I can examine, share, and build on. If a language model can capture some of the reasoning behind those decisions, it could help another researcher navigate an experiment, and it could also help me question my own habits. The interesting challenge is whether it can learn when a piece of advice applies, rather than simply repeat what I would say.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of experimental know-how is difficult to communicate. You can write down the procedure, but that doesn’t necessarily capture why you made a particular choice, what you noticed when something went wrong, or how you decided what to try next. Much of that stays in the researcher’s head.

I want to externalize that knowledge so it becomes something we can question, share, and improve. A language model could help make those judgments explicit. Someone could ask, “Why did you do this?” or “What would you try if this failed?” and explore the reasoning behind the experiment.

For me, the interesting part is also discovering what I actually know. When you try to explain your intuition, you find gaps and assumptions you hadn’t noticed. The model’s suggestions would still need to be tested, but that process could help turn individual experience into knowledge other people can build on.
